cells.tense: The light is here now, and it came from what was actually built.
cells.ask: Show one piece of what you've been holding back, at the edge of what feels ready. Let it stand where it is today.
cells.core:
You can be bright without it running you. There's a way of holding attention — in what you make, in what you say, in the figure you cut — that doesn't ask you to keep proving or keep reaching. It stays level. People feel that before they can name it, and it's what makes the work land.

You can also read the room. Being in the middle of a mess doesn't stop you from taking the next step. Something in you knows which piece is unfinished and which is fine, and acts on that. What's been cultivated here has actually reached something. The shine is that arriving, not the chase. Take the next step and let the shape stay open.
cells.sheetLine: What you've built is light in the room, and you can look at it.
cells.verb: the pull toward the light you keep returning to
cells.place: where the road hasn't closed yet

cells.tense: You're pushed into a future where this already worked, and you've left the room you're standing in.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's here — no waiting. Finish it in the shape it has. Then say one line about what you noticed, out loud.
cells.core:
You're staring past the current thing at a future one you can already half-see. The enthusiasm is real, and it's arriving a beat early — jumping past the work, landing on the version where it's already done and already bright. That version doesn't exist yet, and pushing toward it is what's costing you.

If the future version stays unbuilt for one day, what actually happens? Not forever — the pull toward what's really wanted isn't the problem. The problem is that you're watching ahead of yourself instead of the page. Some of the light you're hunting is already under your hands. Let what's here be enough for today.
cells.sheetLine: The picture ahead keeps you from finishing what's here.
cells.verb: the pull toward the light you keep returning to

cells.tense: You hoped, you tried, and the flowering never came the way you were told it would.
cells.ask: Pick one living thing under your hands — a plant, a person, a skill — and give it care today without checking whether it worked.
cells.core:
You spent something on this and it did not resolve into the shape you expected. Somewhere along the way the light stopped being a direction and became a story you were tired of hearing. The pull is still there — you can feel it on a good day — but you're not trusting it with anything real anymore.

What's gone isn't the wish for it. It's the energy to keep wishing on credit. There's a way back through tending, not striving. Find the small living thing under your hands and keep giving it something, no proof required. The light comes back as a side effect of care, not as a reward for it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped trusting what you wanted. Something smaller can still be tended.

cells.tense: You're already giving off light and you'd talk about it as if it weren't yours.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did this week that helped someone and call it yours, quietly, to yourself first. Then say it to one person who saw it.
cells.core:
There's a thing you do that others notice before you do — you steady, you brighten, you keep going in a way that helps. Someone told you, maybe, and you waved it off. Or you used to have it and you stopped, and the absence is what you're living now, unnamed. Either way, you're not tracking the fact of it.

You can keep giving what you give without having to prove anything. Saying it out loud doesn't add weight; it lets you keep going without pretending. You get to know what you're doing and still do it plainly, and that's a kind of relief.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the light in the room. Saying so is the work.

attempts.check: Two soft spots. First, about the Too Little cell: I say the person got out ahead of what they could still see, and the record only supports 'cultivation that never flowered' — that the flowering never came. I can locate the exhaustion against the person's own past attempts, but the record doesn't tell me how long ago, what they tried, or who else was in the room; I must not supply any of that. Second, a reader of the Balanced cell could reasonably say the radiance comes from something outside the person — luck, an unusually good year, people who backed them — and I can't prove it's cultivation. The ask holds either way: showing one piece at the edge of what's ready is useful even if my reading of where the light comes from is wrong. The line I had to cut is 'the star is yours' — it sounds like something worth keeping and it serves the cell, not the person.
